text: Good evening, everyone. Can we go ahead and grab a seat?

Thank you, and welcome to our 2026/2027 school year and first meeting for SEAC. Obviously, I am your SEAC chair, Erin Rozelle Poe, and I'm very honored to be here with all of you today. Before we jump into our kickoff event, there are some delicious goodies all the way in the back, if anybody has not seen

them, done by Laura Colosi over here. She always provides such yummy treats for us. So please help yourselves. I was just speaking with Dr. Spence, and it's truly hard to believe that we are in our fourth week of school. It just feels like it's flown by. It's amazing. So also, before I forget, and we'll flash it again, if you haven't done so, please scan the QR code.

Basically, let us know that you're here. And then if you haven't had a chance, there are flyers on the back of the table, as well as if there are any public comments this evening, the sign-up is on the back as well. And at this time, we'll go ahead and get started with our superintendent, Dr. Aaron Spence. Well, good evening. Good evening.

So nice to be here with you. It's true, the four weeks have felt very fast, but they've also, in some ways, felt very long. Which is probably a bit like being married. I am very glad to be here with you all. It's always a pleasure to spend some time with this team, with this group of people, the wonderful educators, parents, family members in the room.

We, I think really appreciate and need you to hear from me that we really appreciate the questions that you ask us. When we start thinking about how we're meeting the needs of our kids, they're really important and meaningful conversations for us to get into. And I always want to just start the conversation with you all with an expression of gratitude because it really does make us better. It makes us better at our work.

It makes us more empathetic in how we think about what we do for our kids. It helps us really hone in on the strategies that are important strategies for making a difference in the lives of the kids that we serve. And that, of course, is all kids, but certainly for this environment, our students with disabilities. And I'm proud of a lot of that work, and I hope that you are proud of a lot of that work. So I don't know. How many folks are sort of new-ish to this group? Not many.

Everybody's pretty-- Just a few. It's okay. You can raise your hand. Welcome. We're glad you're here. Yes, we're glad you're here. So maybe you won't know some of this, but the other folks who've been in the room for a while will know some of the really good things that have been happening, and I want to talk a little bit about that. I do want to celebrate growth. I do want to say, at the outset, as we're looking at what's going on with the testing environment,

and what's going on at the state with accountability, we are seeing growth. So what we're doing is working in our schools, but I also want to acknowledge, without any hesitation and no excuse-making, that the gaps that we see in learning for our students with disabilities remain far too high. So we know there's still a lot of work to do. And that's why we're here. We're here to attack that with vigor and with seriousness, and to try to understand what else we need to be doing together to ensure that we're meeting the needs of the kids that we serve.

But I also know we don't define success only by what's happening on those assessments. I hope we don't define success for our children based on what's happening on our assessments, right? We were talking about our own kids, and so I now have my last two. So those of you who've been with SEAC for a while know I have a lot of children. And my last two, I've got now a freshman in high school and a senior in high school. And I know. Isn't that nuts? It makes me so sad.

I no longer have any kids in middle school or elementary school. But I'm thinking about my senior, as I say we don't define our kids only by assessment. He does fine in school. His grades are fine. We've been talk-- The senior years, when you start having a lot of conversations about what comes next, and he made this really interesting decision at the beginning of the summer. He came to us, he said, "Mom, Dad, I'm not going to go to

college." I said, "Okay, tell me more." He would be our first not to go to college. I said, "Tell me more." He said, "I want to fly airplanes. And I met a pilot who said, 'Don't go to college. There's another path.'" And he started talking to us about that path. And so this summer, he started working on his private pilot's license, and he's following a different path for himself. And really, that's the thing that we need to be doing for all of our kids, right? We need to be thinking about where are your passions and what is your pathway, and

how do we connect those things together and make sure that those opportunities exist here in our schools and that they exist for all of our kids. And that's why I remain, again, proud of the work we do in LCPS, but really proud of the work that you all do to keep pushing us. I'll give you just one example we celebrated last night at our school board meeting, if you happened to be watching it. Without SEAC, we're not building independent living labs or apartments,

which we are now building in our schools. And we had the chance to hear from the folks at Rockridge last night to talk about not only to see what it looks like, but to talk about the difference that it's making for the kids who are learning about independence and what it means to be out on your own and find your pathway in the world, but do that in a safe place where the adults around them can help them navigate some of those challenges. And I just thought, man, that is so cool and so exciting. And then as I was sitting there, I was like, "Oh, good.

I get to go to SEAC tomorrow. I've got to tell them we got to see that." Because truly, it was the push that you all gave for us to be able to talk with our board during the capital improvement process and put those labs into the capital plan and make that a reality. So something for all of us to be proud about. And then other stuff that's going on that I hope you know about, I know you know about, but just to highlight. The VIEW Transition Academy.

We had a presentation last night on our capital program, and if you saw that presentation, you saw the rendering of the Transition Academy and you saw the conversation. If you like really firm budgets, you won't love this part of it because we basically doubled the budget for the thing because of the programming that we want to put in there. Because after we said, "This is what we think it'll cost for the building," we've literally doubled the budget to put the right

programming in. And we've done that programming by talking with our students, by talking with you all, with our parents and our families, by talking with our educators and saying, "What needs to be in the world's best transition center?" And then we put that in writing, and we said, "This is our plan, and so we're going to find a way to pay for it." And that's in our budget, and that is going to open in August of '28. If you think about that, that's amazing, right? So that's just-

... not that far away. And it's going to be world-class, and it's going to be the best transition center in the country, and we're going to show other people how to do it. Fifteen career pathways have been identified for that transition center. Opportunities for kids to come and learn with professionals, learn with business partners, learn with each other about how to go into the world and live a fulfilling life. And what a blessing that is for us to be able to offer that

opportunity. But that does not happen without you all. SEAC was the impetus behind that transition center, pushing Tedra, who likes to push me, who likes to push the board to say, "This is something we should do." And I say that to say what happens in here really does matter. And so if you're frustrated at times, and you will be

I know you will because I am. If you're concerned at times, because you will be, if you're wondering why you, after a long day of doing all the other things you do, spend time coming in here to advocate for children, just remember that what you're doing in here really matters, and it is making a difference in our school division, and it does help hold us accountable, and it does help remind us that we need to

really dig in and make sure that we're being the best that we can be. And that's through your advocacy. It's through your policy, and governance feedback. It's through the way that you push us on budget. I was just telling Erin we have a budget retreat with our school board next week, so we're already starting the new budget process, and we'll be talking to them about priorities. And one thing I know every year is I'm going to hear from SEAC

about some budget priorities, and it's going to be about how are we appropriately staffing our schools to meet the needs of our kids and we'll continue to try to prioritize that as we have done over the last three years of budgets that I've been able to put together here in LCPS with our school board. We have prioritized. Now we haven't met every need, and we won't meet every need this year because budgets are what budgets are, and there's always choices. But we will continue to expand and to grow and to make sure that the programs that

need to be in place are in place, and that the support systems that are in place for our kids. Before I wrap up, because I know we have a lot of other folks who want to talk to you, I do want to push to an advocacy agenda item for just a second. I haven't brought it up with you all yet, so I'm going to bring it up now because it's really been weighing on my mind a lot. So if you're familiar with a program called E-Rate. So E-Rate, it's a federal program,

and it goes through the FCC, the Federal Communications Commission. It is a program that funds connectivity in schools. It's really its sole purpose is to make sure that internet exists in schools. So it funds hardware. It funds broadband. It started several decades ago. When it started, about 12% of the nation's schools had the internet, and now about 95% of our nation's schools have the internet.

And it is really directly because of federal E-Rate funding that that happens. There's a swinging scale of reimbursement ability that you get from E-Rate, depending on how much your community is able to afford. So for Loudoun, we're fairly blessed, as everybody here knows, and we get about a 50% reimbursement rate on our purchases. There are districts, and so this is an advocacy beyond our borders, but it's something that I want help with. There are many districts, particularly in rural

communities and across the Commonwealth and across the country, who rely solely on this funding for internet connectivity. And, there's a proposed rulemaking that's going on right now. They're seeking comment, and they are considering narrowing dramatically the scope of E-Rate or sunsetting it altogether. And so I've been having this conversation in our business community because I want us to imagine what it would look like to try to hire somebody who comes out of our

schools, having never had any meaningful experience with technology. That would be an awkward situation for our employers who rely on technology every day to solve their problems. But I think for this group, one of the things that struck me when I was talking with a friend about this the other day was what about our kids who rely on adaptive devices? What about our kids whose modifications and accommodations require the use of technology to learn? What about the way we're trying to level the playing field with those technologies for our kids?

What about the way we communicate, the way we develop IEPs, all of those things that we do that require... So I know we don't all love screens. We shouldn't all love screens all the time, but there are productive and responsible uses for screens, and for many of the kids that we serve, they're critical. And I worry deeply about our nation's children when things like this happen without a lot of thought. And unfortunately, one of the things we're seeing is that a lot of the decisions

being made at the federal level about public education, in particular, are happening without a great deal of thought. And so what I want is for part of my job and my role I see is to make sure that you're aware of that, because there is an opportunity to offer comment. And you can go, if you just look up proposed rulemaking FCC E-Rate, you can go to the page where you can submit those comments, and I would just encourage you all to talk about that from an advocacy lens, Erin, if you don't

mind, about whether or not you want to submit comment on behalf of the students that we serve who may be impacted by that, not just here in Loudoun County, but across the Commonwealth and across the country. Because our kids need us, and walking away from programs like that is not a solution to our problem. So anyway, with that, that was not the intention to come up here and do that tonight, but I was writing a letter to submit for comments over the last two days, and since it's been on my mind, I thought I would share it with you as well.

It is an honor and a privilege to serve as the superintendent of Loudoun County. It's my fourth year now as superintendent, which is just hard to believe. But it is an honor and a privilege to serve here because of you, because of our community. I tell people all the time, I live and work in the best community for education in the country, not because of our schools, but because of the people who live in and invest in our schools, and that's you guys. So thanks for everything that you do for us. We appreciate you.

Thank you so much, Dr. Spence. And again, we really do appreciate everything that you do for SEAC as well as for all of our students here in LCPS. Next up, I would like to welcome Ms. Tedra Richardson. Good evening. How are you? Good. Good. Did everybody have a nice summer? Thumbs up.

Okay, good. We have a room full of thumbs up. That's awesome. I hope your school year is off to a strong and meaningful start. It is wonderful to see you all for this kickoff meeting this afternoon, so thank you for being here. I'm going to share some happenings from across the Department of Student Services. So starting us off, our Office of Diagnostic and Prevention Services is launching a new professional learning experience for

our educators, for our TAs, and it is called Strong Adults, Strong Schools. So we do a lot of focus and a lot of support on our students, but we also have to take care of ourselves to be able to pour into them. And so when you get this presentation, you can click the link. You can see what those experiences are going to be for our staff members throughout this school year. So we're very excited about this opportunity for them.

From the Office of Student Services, oh my gosh, we have a partnership with HealthWorks, Dr. Tonya Atkins, and she applied for a state grant in partnership with LCPS, and we were awarded the full grant. We have two vehicles. You can see one of them there in this picture. We have one for free dental services and one for free medical services

for our students in LCPS. We are so excited. Yes, absolutely. And we will make sure that we have a kickoff experience and a ribbon cutting. We got the vehicles a lot faster than what we thought we were going to. So we're super excited to get this up and running. We should have a soft start by the end of October, start of November, and we're

going to start with a handful of schools out in the east, but we're really looking to expand this really to all of our regions across LCPS. Special education, our SIFs, have really partnered with Teaching and Learning, and we now, as a division, have an LCPS coaching model, a cycle that we are working collaboratively with our friends in Teaching and Learning in

partnership with the Department of School Leadership and really having meaningful impact in supporting our teachers, in providing mentoring, modeling, feedback, and really looking at our student progress. So we're excited about that. Student mental health services, we are going to start really looking at and logging our responsive services. So certainly, we can log into our student information

system now. We can go to student conference logs, and we can pull that information, but really having it all in one place by discipline. So our school psychs, our school social workers, our school counselors, and our student assistant specialists, and really having meaningful, planned, and intentional dialogue around what is this data telling us? What are the trends that we're seeing in our responsive services when we're meeting with

students so we can better tailor and target our supports to students, schools, and families? And then out of procedural support, our school board was supportive of five additional ment training positions, and we have had a huge impact with training to start this school year. We got a lot of training done over the summer, so people were well-positioned to

kick off the school year. Safety is always a priority for us, making sure that everyone feels safe within our educational settings, and so we're happy to celebrate that. Dr. Spence did preview a little bit of what's going on with our View Transition Academy, but we are slated to host our second roundtable on October 2nd. And yes, this is the visual of what it will look

like when all is said and done. It has been an exciting process. It has been overwhelming at times. There are details that have to be thought about that you don't always think of because we typically just get to walk into school buildings and everything is up and running and functioning, but we're building it from the ground up. Our focus for our roundtable on October 2nd is having

our businesses that were there with us for the original kickoff in May of 2025, coming back to join us, and then we have a host of new businesses that are going to be joining us. And we have structured our time together to really look at these three bullets. Looking at curriculum and skill alignment. Are we on track with what we have identified in our 15 pathways?

Is it going to have meaning and purpose for our students once they age out of this opportunity that we're creating for them? Work-based learning. What are our new businesses and current business partners willing to commit? So we're going to be having them to complete some commitment cards and give them the opportunity to ask those questions in a safe space. Maybe I don't know what it's like to work with a person with a disability.

We want them to be able and be comfortable to ask those questions, to share what they may perceive as some challenges or how they might need some support from us to make sure that our students, once they enter the workforce, are successful. And then looking at those community and civic partnerships, just how can we build those sustainable relationships and onboard many more businesses for which our students can go out and join the workforce?

I will say that your SEAC leadership team has been integral in adding businesses to those lists. I tell you one thing, you put SEAC on something, and you guys are going to get it done. So thank you. Thank you. We definitely appreciate all of your support. We do have SEAC leadership that have been invited to the roundtable on October 2nd. So in addition to us sharing some of that feedback, I know that the leadership team

will as well. Again, thank you for joining us this evening. Thank you for your partnership. Thank you for your passion. Thank you for your care, and thank you for continuing to show up for not just your students, our students, but also showing up for us. Have a good evening. Next up, I'd like to welcome Ms. Nikia Pernell from the Office of Special Education.

So I'm not snitching, but Liz was already trying to steal your picture to get more businesses. I told her Amy was in the back. I wouldn't be approving that. So Amy, Liz will be coming to talk to you about the proper way to create communications to businesses. Thank you, Liz. Always on the job. Always on the job. Welcome back. Welcome back. Welcome back. Welcome back.

Are we ready? Are we ready? Are we energized? So I just want to say welcome back. Last year, we did so many good things together. We did a lot of work around belonging, connection, and our shared responsibilities. We had a lot of nice connection activities throughout last school year. It reminded us that belonging is more than simply being invited into the space. What do we call that? Breathing the what? Gen Ed.

The Gen Ed air. It's more than just breathing the Gen Ed air, right? Belonging means that we're being seen, heard, valued, knowing that our voice means something, and that we can all make a difference no matter who we are. We talked a lot about that last year. It also means creating space for different experiences, different opinions, different perspectives, different ideas, different cultures, and just approaching

those things with curiosity and most importantly, respect. Right? So this year, we will continue to build on that foundation. I will not be the one doing the connection, sadly, but it will keep going. Our goal is going to be continuing to grow SEAC as a true collaborative team. Over the last couple of years, two or three years, we have turned what used to be more of a debate and a lot of contention into friendships, partnerships.

We fellowship here. We come here. We share treats. We share stories. We talk about our kids. So we truly have transformed this into a collaborative space, and we want to keep that momentum going because we want to continue to see the seats get filled. Sometimes we will come in, and the supervisors in SEAC will be making up the whole crew, so continue to invite your friends because our goal is to continue having more families, educators, administrators, community partners,

and guess what? Children. Children are a part of SEAC. We have children who are old enough to have a voice. They participate in their transition meetings. We want to hear from them. They are the customer. So we'd like to see some children start filling some of these seats this year, and we're going to kick off this year with some promises. I'm just going to read them. We're going to put them on some little cards, and we'll share these promises. If you disagree, you can write your comments on the back, and I may or may not have a comment box.

But we shall see. So first, connecting before we problem solve, which is why we always have that connection. We got a little busy a couple of times, and the connection got pushed to the back. But we will make sure that we intentionally prioritize that connection because our relationships matter. Those strong relationships are what make a difference when we have to have those hard or courageous conversations outside of this particular environment. Creating space for every voice.

Again, different perspectives is what strengthens our collective work. So every voice in this room matters, and we will respect every voice in the room. Listening with curiosity. You know how we always tell our kids and our spouses, "Don't listen to respond." I can tell you're just trying to get your rebuttal together. This is not a debate. We are listening for curiosity, listening to ask questions for clarification, listening to learn from one another, because

we learn something new every day. Moving from concerns to collaboration. How many times do I tell y'all when you all bring a concern? Is it three or is it 3,000? Now, we care about three, but three is in a division-wide problem. Three, we can go directly to the source. 3,000, that means we got to get moving. We got to delegate some teams. We got to do some research. We got to figure it out. So again, making sure we're not making mountains out of molehills, right?

That we're really considering things and being intentional about where we put our energy because it's only so many of us to do the work, and we don't want to burn out focusing on things that all students and families don't benefit from, that just benefit maybe one or two, right? Or one area in particular and not the entire division. And then building belonging through action. So again, the way we communicate, collaborate, and show up for one another is a

part of the culture we're not just modeling when we come here, but that we're creating for the rest of the division and our schools because when they see us come together and they go, "All those advocates, all those attorneys coming in, are they friends? Why are they laughing together?" Because that's what we do. We can have spirited debates. We can have courageous conversations. We can respect one another's difference of opinion, and then we can come together and collaborate and do great things like View Transition Academy, which we worked

really closely together on and pushed across the line. So most importantly, we just want SEAC meetings to feel like a place where people know they belong, and they know their contribution matters. So please continue to show up and bring a friend and bring a kid. It would be great to see kids here. So a little bit of information. This is officially our first SEAC meeting. I would like to introduce our new assistant director, my twin, Bridget Gorie.
She will be in charge of connecting moving forward. We also have two... Oh, not two, four, double that. Four new supervisors who've joined our team, Jamar Brown. RJ Horstmeyer. Jessica Pellegrino.

And Christina Schmidt. We have added such a wealth of knowledge to our team, such diversity. They all bring very distinct gifts, and so we have grown our team in such a special way, and just very excited about that. We do also have an exciting new resource. It is not division-wide, but we've done a little bit of focusing on our TSI, so our targeted support schools and our comprehensive support schools that have been

federally identified under ESSA, which you guys know is the Every Student Succeeds Act. So we've had some schools identified as TSI and CSI schools. So we have adopted Touch Math, which is a concrete multisensory approach to learning math skills, which a lot of our students need, basically pairing those numbers with those tactile and visual resources to enhance the learning of our students and give them a different way to approach learning math.

We will be closely tracking. Again, this was grant funded, so we will be closely tracking this pilot this year, the outcomes and the growth, so that we can make decisions to move forward toward expansion in the future. So maybe there will be some opportunities during our specialized instruction subcommittees where we might be able to see some of those resources, so you can see what it looks like, feels like, maybe see some of those tactile resources.

So that's really exciting news for the students in those identified schools. And then we have some new supports for school teams. In a response to behavior, I know post-COVID, we've talked a lot about behavior. Behaviors have changed. We say, "We've never seen children like this." Those who have been around 30, 40, even 50 years are like, "Woo, this is a new breed." So

again, in response to what teams need, especially with so many provisionally licensed teachers, contracted teachers, novice zero to three year teachers, we wanted to make sure that our office was being responsive with the support. While we already have a lot of specialized instructional facilitators, our coordinators, our specialists, our supervisors, myself, and Bridget, lots of

resources in our office that can come out and support, but we realize sometimes teams are just in crisis, and they don't only need help with behavior, they need help with classroom systems. They need help with visuals. They need help with putting academics into place, ensuring schedules are into place, modeling, coaching, and so that's all hands on deck. So through taking all of the different specialized instructional facilitators,

those who specialize in instruction, those who specialize in behavior, those who specialize in students in specialized programs, and bringing those teams together. We will be coming into schools for up to four weeks to help stabilize those environments and then move on to the next team that requires our help. So that is a new approach that we have started to be responsive to some of the behaviors that you guys have been reporting in your schools and buildings.

And so we'll be also taking data on that. So if we want to expand that, we might have a new budget ask. I'm not sure. But certainly, we'll ask SEAC to support that request should we need that, and we know that you will. I do believe that is all for me, other than, look at this. We're serving 10,482 students with disabilities, with 180 students in initial eligibility.

So while they say things are stabilizing, we just keep growing and growing and growing. So we want to make sure that we continue this relationship so we can continue learning from one another, teaching one another, lifting one another up because we got work to do. Do you see how many students this is? We still didn't hit 11,000. We almost hit it, so we'll see where we are by the end

of the year. But I appreciate you all. I'm very excited to be here tonight. I'm so very excited to hear the policies. Maybe I was kidding. I'm not sure, but I thought they would get a kick out of it. I don't see Craig. I thought he would laugh from the back, but he's not here. So you guys, Melissa, you'll have to text him and tell him I said that. All right. So who is next up? Ms. Rae Mitchell, Chief of Schools.
Come on down. Good evening, everyone. Thank you for inviting me to my very first SEAC meeting ever. Yay.

So I was invited to just give an overview of my department, which is the Department of School Leadership, or DOSL as we're commonly known as, and we work very closely alongside the Department of Student Services as we support all of the students in LCPS. So I have five departments in DOSL. We have three level offices.

We also have the Office of School Administration, and then we have the Office of Athletics and Student Activities. So in the slides that you're going to see, I'm just going to go over some names or show you who the directors are and the executive principals in the event that you as parents and/or employees will have contacts with the different people

in these departments. You will have the most contact with the level offices and at times, the Office of School Administration. While the Office of Athletics and Student Activities supports all students, you probably won't have as much contact with that office as some of the others. So in the Office of Elementary Education, we have a new director this year, Kevin West, and we have four executive principals.

We support 60 elementary schools and the two charters, and we have a virtual distance learning program for elementary students that that office also supports. For middle school, I'm sorry, I went too fast. For middle school, we also have a new director, Ms. Mildred Charlie Green, and we have one executive principal, which is Ms. Robinson. We have 18 middle schools, and we also have students in our virtual Loudoun

program at the middle school level. And then in high school, our director, Ms. Nettie Gonzalez Sales, we have two executive principals, and they support the 18 high schools and the six alternative programs, such as TAPE, which is the Alternative Education Program, RISE, which you may be familiar with, Academies of Loudoun, all of our non-comprehensive school sites, Robey.

And the VIEW Transition Academy will be a part of that, that we will support in our level offices as well. And we also have students involved in the virtual Loudoun program. The Office of School Administration, Ms. Dana Scanlon is our director, and we have a supervisor, Dr. Jefferson, and we have one hearing officer, Ms. Williams, who you may be familiar with, who was our former ombuds.

And she's now in the Office of School Administration. That office works very closely with Ms. LaBelle, with our Student Behavior and Accountability Committee. The Office of School Administration handles all of our discipline and our hearings for all of our students. And again, they also work closely with the Office of Special Education when we have students that are found to be in violation of something and they're special education students. So that is another office that works very closely with OSE.

And then our office of athletics and student activities. Our director is Mr. Derek Ferry. Dr. and John Poturo is one of our supervisors, and then Ms. Chuy, who is also new, is for student clubs and activities. So again, all of our students that are involved in any intramural sports at the middle school level, our freshmen, junior varsity, and varsity athletics at the

high school level, and then all of the clubs that we have in schools are supported by this particular office. So we do a lot of things to get student interest involved in our schools during the school day and after school. And we are also having two other people that are not necessarily a part of our office, but they support DASL, and that's Mr. Hudson, who is our coordinator for parent and stakeholder services.

So if you've ever filled out one of those Let's Talk or OnFlow submissions, depending on what is submitted, it comes to our office, and he triages those and works with the various departments to get you responses that you need in a timely manner. And Ms. Hamilton is also fairly new. So she is the coordinator that supports all of our summer programs and after-school programs, which will be expanding from elementary to middle and high school for the

summer of 2027. So that is an overview of the Department of School Leadership. Again, because we support all of our schools and all of our students, we collaborate with multiple departments to ensure that our students are getting the support that they need. And we are going to be working a lot closer with special education this year, as Ms.

Richardson and I have weekly meetings, and we're looking at how to better collaborate to make sure that we are being proactive, particularly for our students with disabilities. Thank you. Thank you, everybody, for your overviews and also being here for the kickoff

portion. At this time, we've gone ahead and identified all of our school board members by their districts, but at this time, I also want to acknowledge a few of our school board members that are here. We have Carrie LaBelle, who's our liaison, and then also up here with us this evening is Ms. April Chandler. She is our chair of the school board. Do we have any other school board members in attendance this evening?
